previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient was admitted with a flare of chronic pancreatitis and associated epigastric pain radiating to the back, along with nausea, vomiting, and inability to tolerate J-tube feeds. She also reported atypical chest pain radiating to the left arm, which was exacerbated by nausea and vomiting but relieved by sublingual nitroglycerin. Workup showed no cardiac ischemia, with normal EKGs and negative troponins, suggesting the chest pain may have been due to esophageal spasm. She was managed with IV fluids, pain control using Dilaudid, Ativan, and Phenergan per her established protocol, and NPO status. A PICC line was placed on hospital day three for reliable IV access. Her symptoms improved over five days, she resumed J-tube feeds, and was discharged on her baseline medications with follow-up arranged. No further chest pain occurred after admission day one.

Brief Hospital Course:
___ year old female with chronic pancreatitis, migraines, severe 
depression (with prior suicide attempts), HTN who presents with 
seizures in the setting of pancreatitis flare and abuse of 
tramadol, benzos, seroquel, and fioricet.  

# Seizures: patient with three clonic-tonic seizures (one three 
weeks ago at home, one the day prior to admission, and one in 
the ED). Provoking factors including sleep deprivation and 
decreased po intake from her pancreatitis flare and polydrug 
abuse including Tramadol, benzodiazepine, seroquel, and 
fioricet. MRI shows no acute changes or seizure focus. EEG shows 
no seizure activity but slowing at left temporal region, which 
can increase her risk for seizures. Patient had no seizures 
throughout hospitalization. Per neurology recommendations, she 
was started on keppra 750mg BID and has follow up with neurology 
as an outpatient. Plan is to switch to Lamictal as an outpatient 
since it is also a mood stabilizer and requires monitoring while 
titrating up the drug. 

# Abdominal pain: idiopathic chronic Pancreatitis diagnosis 
confirmed by secretin testing-- peak bicarb 54 in ___, however 
previous CT abdomen and MRCP with no evidence of acute or 
chronic pancreatitis. She has the classic symptom of epigastric 
pain radiating to back with multiple hospitalizations. Lipase 
was normal during admission, but can remain normal in setting of 
chronic pancreatitis. She was started on her usual pancreatitis 
treatment protocol established at prior admissions.  
-- NPO except meds  
-- Normal saline at 100 ml/hr  
-- Dilaudid 2 mg IV Q3H:PRN pain  
-- Dilute Dilaudid in NS 50 ml and infuse over 15 minutes.

-- Promethazine 25 mg IV Q6H:PRN nausea  
-- Lorazepam 1 mg IV Q4H:PRN nausea or anxiety  
-- Lorazepam 1 mg IV HS:PRN insomnia   
Patient was then transitioned to dilaudid po and her femoral 
line was removed. At discharge, she reported improvement of her 
pain. Her nausea was also well controlled and she was able to 
eat all meals.

benzos, tramadol, seroquel, fioricet, methadone. Her tox screen 
was positive for methadone, although not prescribed. Patient 
able to refill pills at various pharmacies. Meetings with

PRN) and lorazepam 1mg BID PRN, 7 days supply with no refills.

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST RADIOGRAPH

HISTORY:  Possible seizure.

COMPARISONS:  ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Chest, AP semi-upright view.

FINDINGS:  The cardiac, mediastinal and hilar contours appear unchanged.  The
lungs appear clear.  There are no pleural effusions or pneumothorax.

IMPRESSION:  No evidence of acute disease.

STUDY:  MRI of the brain with and without contrast.

CLINICAL INDICATION:  ___ woman with history of chronic pancreatitis
and migraines, admitted for several possible seizures, evaluate for seizure
focus.

COMPARISON:  Prior head CT dated ___ and prior MRI of the
maxillofacial structures dated ___.

TECHNIQUE:  Pre-contrast sagittal T1, axial FLAIR, axial T2, axial magnetic
susceptibility and axial diffusion-weighted images were obtained through the
brain.  Axial T1-weighted images with gadolinium contrast were obtained. 
High-resolution coronal T2-weighted images and also coronal T1-weighted
sequences with contrast were obtained.

FINDINGS:  There is no evidence of acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass, mass
effect, or shifting of the normally midline structures.  The ventricles and
sulci are normal in size and configuration for the patient's age.  The T2 and
FLAIR sequences, demonstrates few scattered foci of high signal intensity,
distributed in the subcortical and periventricular white matter, which are
nonspecific and may reflect areas of small vessel disease.  No diffusion
abnormalities are detected to suggest acute or subacute ischemic changes. 
There is no evidence of abnormal enhancement.  The high-resolution images
throughout the temporal lobes are partially limited due to patient motion;
however, there is no evidence of mesial temporal sclerosis or cortical
heterotopia.  The major vascular flow voids are present and demonstrate normal
distribution.  The orbits are unremarkable, the paranasal sinuses are clear as
well as the mastoid air cells.

IMPRESSION: 1.  There is no evidence of acute intracranial process, no
diffusion abnormalities are detected to suggest acute or subacute ischemic
changes, there is no evidence of abnormal enhancement.

2.  Few scattered foci of high signal intensity are detected in the
subcortical and periventricular white matter on the T2 and FLAIR sequences,
which are nonspecific and may reflect chronic microvascular ischemic disease.

3.  The high-resolution images throughout the temporal lobes are grossly
unremarkable, there is no evidence of mesial temporal sclerosis or cortical
heterotopia.
